first_impression.reaction: Sophie: The grandmother opening is nice and it doesn't do 'fairytale Portugal' at me, which I appreciate. The line that hooked me was 'several customs repeated online have no Portuguese source at all.' That's the kind of honesty we never get from wedding sites. We're not Portuguese though, so I skimmed the traditions and read the legal and guest sections properly, because Portugal is on our shortlist.

journey.quote: Portuguese wedding traditions are quieter and more local than most lists suggest, and several customs repeated online have no Portuguese source at all.
journey.reaction: Straight away this feels like someone has actually checked things. I'd trust the rest more because of this.

journey.section: The Minho bride in black and Viana gold filigree
journey.quote: One practical detail for brides wearing a family heirloom: traditional Portuguese gold is 19.2 carat.
journey.reaction: Nice insider detail, the sort of thing I'd screenshot. Not relevant to us personally, but it tells me the writer knows the country rather than rewriting a listicle.

journey.section: The groom's tie and the bride's shoe
journey.quote: Neither is documented as old or universal, so ask before you plan either.
journey.reaction: Good. James would cringe at a shoe-passing money thing in front of our friends, and this gives us permission to skip it without feeling we've disrespected anyone.

journey.section: Before the wedding / The wedding day
journey.quote: In villages, the bride is often told to walk to the church with her family and guests rather than arrive by car.
journey.reaction: By this point 'often told' has turned up a lot. I respect the honesty, but in the middle third I started skimming because so much is hedged that I wasn't sure what's actually real.

journey.section: Bringing Portuguese wedding traditions to a wedding in Australia
journey.quote: Australian venues often run to a set finish time, so if your family expects a late, unhurried copo-d'água, raise it early when you compare venues.
journey.reaction: Practical and honest trade-off. More of this please.

journey.section: Marrying legally in Portugal as an Australian
journey.quote: Smartraveller notes that Portuguese government pages in English are often out of date or inaccurate, so confirm current requirements directly.
journey.reaction: As a lawyer I really like this. It's upfront about the limits of the information instead of pretending it's simple.

journey.section: Documents and the Australian Embassy in Lisbon
journey.quote: The embassy says the marriage must take place within three months of approval; IRN and the Justice portal say six months.
journey.reaction: Flagging the conflict between sources is exactly what I'd want. It also makes me think: this is the bit we'd pay someone to sort out so we're not chasing a registry office in Portuguese.

journey.section: Civil registration at the Conservatória do Registo Civil
journey.quote: Online applications are only open to Portuguese citizens (and some Brazilian nationals) with Portuguese digital ID, so most Australians start in person or through a representative with a special power of attorney.
journey.reaction: This raises the question I actually care about: do we have to fly to Portugal to start this, or can the Advisor's team act as the representative? The page stops just short of telling me.

journey.section: Travel and safety notes for guests
journey.quote: Biometric registration on arrival under the EU Entry/Exit System can slow the border, especially at Lisbon airport. Build time into guest transfers.
journey.reaction: This is our grandparents-from-the-airport worry in one line. Real logistics detail. I'd forward this section to Mum.

journey.section: Marrying legally in Portugal as an Australian (CTA)
journey.quote: You have one Advisor as a single point of contact from start to finish, and the fee is agreed in writing before any work begins.
journey.reaction: Fee agreed in writing before any work is exactly what eases the hidden-costs worry. 'Single point of contact' is better than the usual 'end-to-end', though I still want to know who actually turns up on the day in Portugal.

unanswered_questions: Can Wedded Wonderland handle the in-person registry step or the power of attorney, or do we need to travel to Portugal beforehand?
Who is physically on the ground in Portugal on the day, your own people or local suppliers we never meet?
Is there a real wedding you've done in Portugal (venue and date) we could look at?
Do you help with guest transfers from Lisbon or Porto airport for older guests?
Given the summer heat warning, which months do you actually recommend for an outdoor wedding in Portugal?
would_share_with: James (the legal and guest travel sections)
Sophie's mum, who is helping pay (the Smartraveller and airport delay notes)

cta_reaction.quote: If the paperwork feels like the part that could unravel the plan, speak with a Wedded Advisor.
cta_reaction.why: It's low-pressure and lands right where I'm feeling the paperwork anxiety, which is smart. But we're early, and I'd want to see a real Portugal wedding and read a couple more posts before booking a call. I'd probably click the magazine link first.

top_3_changes: Next to the Advisor CTA, say plainly what you can do on the paperwork for Australians (for example whether you can coordinate the registry step or the representative) so the legal section turns into a reason to enquire.
Link a real Portugal wedding (venue and date) or a Portugal destination page with one, because that's what moves us from reading to enquiring.
Cut back the 'often told' hedging in the wedding-day section, or group the untraceable customs into one short section, so the middle reads faster for skimmers.

checks.check: Every journey point, turn-off and CTA reaction has an exact quote from the draft

No invented brand facts; unknown service details listed as unanswered questions
[[VERIFY]] markers and HTML comments treated as invisible
